headline: The *Anxious* Heart
attribution: Lord, I have carried this long enough. I roll it onto You.
caption:
A prayer for the anxious heart.

Lord, I have carried this long enough.
You never asked me to. I picked it up myself and called it responsibility.
Tonight I roll it onto You: the thing I cannot fix, the person I cannot change, the tomorrow I cannot see.
Let me stop trying to rule the world for one evening.
Hush the wind and the waves inside me the way You hushed them on the lake.
And when I reach to take the burden back, as I will, gently take it from my hands again.
In Jesus' name, amen.

If you are praying this for something specific tonight, you do not have to say what. Just say "me too," and we will pray with you.

headline: A CAPTAIN WOKE AT|MIDNIGHT AND *TURNED*|*HIS SHIP ONE POINT.*|HE HAD NO IDEA WHY.
caption:
He had already set the night's course and gone below.

But as he undressed, one thought would not leave him alone: change the heading. Just one point.

There was no reason for it. The ship was dead on course for port. He lay down and tried to sleep. He couldn't. The impression only pressed harder.

So he climbed back on deck, gave the order, went below, and was asleep the moment his head touched the pillow.

The next day a ship appeared on the horizon. She was sinking. He took off every soul aboard. Soon after, a gale came up and finished her.

One point the other way, and he never would have seen her.

The British government gave that American captain a gold medal. He knew who had really turned the wheel.

Has God ever nudged you to do something that made no sense until later?

headline: BEFORE HE LEFT HOME|FOR THE LAST TIME,|LINCOLN ASKED HIS|NEIGHBORS *FOR ONE THING.*
caption:
Springfield, Illinois. February 11, 1861. Abraham Lincoln stood at the back of a train, about to leave for Washington and a country coming apart.

His neighbors had come to the depot to see him off. He spoke for barely two minutes.

"Here I have lived more than a quarter of a century; here my children were born, and here one of them lies buried. I know not how soon I shall see you again."

Then he told them what he was facing: a duty greater, perhaps, than any man had carried since Washington. And he told them he could not do it alone.

"I hope you, my friends, will all pray that I may receive that Divine assistance, without which I cannot succeed, but with which success is certain."

Not advice. Not votes. Prayer.

The train pulled out. He never saw Springfield again. Four years later it came back carrying his body.

Who is carrying something heavy right now and needs you to do what Lincoln's neighbors were asked to do?

headline: The sick bed is soft *when Thou art there.* The furnace of affliction grows cool *when Thou art there.*
caption:
Spurgeon did not pray for the furnace to be taken away. He prayed for company in it.

He knew the bed and the fire firsthand. He lived with gout, depression, and a wife who was an invalid for most of their marriage.

Where do you need Him to be "there" today?

headline: If we think we love Thee more than we do, we pray that we may yet *love Thee more than we think.*
caption:
Read it slowly. It is one of the most honest sentences ever prayed out loud in front of thousands of people.

He does not claim a great love. He asks for one.

headline: THE CUPBOARD WAS EMPTY.|SHE *PUT THE KETTLE ON*|ANYWAY.
caption:
A London woman set out one clear morning to visit a sick friend in Drury Lane, a basket of tea, butter and food on her arm.

Then the fog came down. So thick the omnibus slowed to a walk. She was deaf, and frightened, and could easily have turned back. Something she could not explain made her go on.

Five flights up, a little girl opened the door. The room was spotless. A tea tray was set. The kettle was boiling.

And there was not a crumb of food in the house.

The daughter had argued that morning: what is the use of boiling water when we have nothing? Her mother would not hear it. God had provided for thirty years, she said. Put the kettle on.

When the basket was opened, the old woman clasped her hands. "You are indeed God's raven, sent by Him to bring us food today. I felt sure He would care for us."

Faith is sometimes just putting the kettle on.

headline: GOD IS NOT SHORT OF WIND. HE MAY BE WAITING FOR SOMEONE TO *SPREAD THE SAILS.*
caption:
A Yorkshire miller once told Sammy Hick there was no wind to grind his corn.

"Spread the cloth," said Sammy. "I'll go and pray."

What sail have you left furled because the air feels dead?

headline: A *Wayward* Child
attribution: They do not look at You, Lord. But do You look at them.
caption:
A prayer for a wayward son or daughter.

Father, You know the name I am holding before You.
They do not look at You. But do You look at them.
Go where I cannot go. Speak where I am no longer heard.
Put someone in their path this week who loves You.
Keep them alive, keep them reachable, and keep me from giving up.
I weep for the one who has no tears for themselves. I pray for the one who has no prayers.
You went after one lost sheep. Go after mine.
In Jesus' name, amen.

The line "They do not look at Thee, but do Thou look at them" comes from a prayer of C. H. Spurgeon.

headline: WOLVES FOLLOWED A|*NINE-YEAR-OLD GIRL*|ALL NIGHT. SHE WALKED|25 MILES UNHARMED.
caption:
She had gone out with her father on a cold November afternoon to bring in the cattle near Platteville, Colorado. He sent her home behind the calves. The calves wandered. By dark she knew she was lost.

Then the wolves came.

They stayed with her all night, growling, close enough to snap at her heels. She kept walking. Eighteen hours. Around twenty-five miles. At ten the next morning she knocked on a stranger's door, unhurt.

When they asked her about it, her answer was simple. Her mother had told her the Lord would always take care of her. So she asked Him to. After that, she said, she knew the wolves would not hurt her, "because God wouldn't let them."

A whole search party was out looking for her. She was home in perfect health.

There is a kind of faith most of us had once and traded for worry. What would it take to get it back?

headline: A WIDOW ASKED HER|PASTOR TO PRAY THAT|*THE WIND WOULD CHANGE.*|HE REFUSED. || Her only son was a sailor. His ship left port that night. *Unless the wind turned.* || She was sure of it: if the wind changed, John would stay for tonight's meeting. *And if he came, he would be converted.* || Her pastor said that was presumptuous. Her answer: "If you cannot join me, *I must pray alone,* for he must stay." || Walking to church that evening, the pastor glanced up at the weather vane. *It had swung around.* || John was sitting in the front row. When he finally sailed, *he sailed a Christian.* The pastor never forgot it.
caption:
Dr. Cleaveland of Boston told this story on himself.

He was willing to pray for the young man's soul. He was not willing to ask God to move the weather for it. That, he told the mother, would be presuming too much.

She did not argue theology with him. She went home and prayed alone.

He admitted afterward that he had learned a lesson that day he never forgot: a praying mother sometimes knows more about what God is willing to do than her minister does.

headline: HE STOOD ON DECK IN|THICK FOG HOLDING A|SUN INSTRUMENT.|*THE CREW JUST STARED.*
caption:
For days the ship had been wrapped in mist. No sun, no stars, no way to fix their position.

Captain Crossby went below and prayed. If he could trust God with his soul, he reasoned, he could trust Him with a ship. Then he asked for one specific thing: a clear sky at twelve o'clock, long enough to take a reading.

At eleven he came on deck with the quadrant under his coat. Drizzle. The men looked at him as if he had lost his mind. He went below and prayed again. Came up again. Nothing.

Ten minutes to twelve. Still gray.

Then, in the old account's words, the mist "seemed to be folded up and rolled away as by an omnipotent and invisible hand." The sun stood in a blue sky. His hands shook so badly he could barely take the reading.

They were on course. And the moment he finished, the mist rolled back over them and the drizzle began again.

He asked for noon. He got noon.

caption:
"Sparsim" is Latin for scattered here and there, the way you would salt a dish.

Henry's point is that prayer is not one item on the day's list. It is seasoning for all the others.

headline: The *Sleepless* Night
attribution: I lay my head to rest on the bosom of Omnipotence.
caption:
A prayer for the sleepless night.

Lord, it is late and my mind will not be quiet.
Every worry I outran today has caught up with me in the dark.
You do not sleep. So there is no reason for both of us to stay awake.
I hand You the night watch.
I lay my head to rest on the bosom of Omnipotence.
Guard this house. Guard the people I love who are under other roofs.
And give Your beloved sleep.
In Jesus' name, amen.

"I lay my head to rest on the bosom of Omnipotence" is Samuel Rutherford's, from the 1600s. It has been putting believers to sleep ever since.

headline: FOR SIX DAYS HIS SHIP|*WOULD NOT MOVE.*|HE ASKED GOD WHY.|THEN HE REACHED PORT.
caption:
He had prayed before sailing from the Kennebec that October, and believed it was right to go.

Then, somewhere off the Bahamas, the ship simply stopped making way. They would sail what felt like thirty or forty miles and find by observation they had gained three or four. Day after day. The captain admitted it tried his faith. "Lord, why are we so hindered?"

At last they broke free and made port.

The first thing people on the dock asked was, "Where have you been through the gale?"

"What gale?"

A hurricane had torn across those waters, leaving wreck and ruin on either side of the patch of sea where he had sat fuming. One ordinary day of sailing would have put him in its path.

"We were anxious to sail on," he said, "but some unseen power held us where we were, and we escaped."

The delay you are praying against may be the answer to a prayer you never knew to pray.

headline: HE CAME TO BUY A TREE.|HE BROUGHT *A BAG OF*|*FLOUR* AND COULDN'T|SAY WHY.
caption:
Central New York, about 1830. Grain was scarce and priced out of reach. In one farmhouse a mother of six sewed for wages as long as her eyes held out, and prayed that God would keep her children from want.

Everyone in the house knew the need. Nobody knew where the answer would come from. Each day the shelf got barer.

Four miles away, a man needed shingles. He decided to buy a pine off their land and split it himself. As he was leaving, a thought stopped him: they might be short of flour. He could not have known. He loaded two bushels anyway.

At the door he almost apologized for it. He had brought some flour toward the price of the tree, he said, in case they could use it.

"That is in answer to prayer," she told him.

Her husband was not a praying man. He believed it too.

When the oldest boy came in that night she had one thing to say: "God has answered our prayers, and sent a bag of flour."

headline: The *Empty* Cupboard
attribution: Lord, You hear when we scrape the bottom of the barrel.
caption:
A prayer for provision.

Father, You see what is in the account and what is due.
I am not asking for riches. I am asking for bread: enough for this day, and the faith not to borrow trouble from the next.
You fed Elijah by ravens. You sent flour to a widow. You hear when we scrape the bottom of the barrel.
Show me the work my hands should do.
Move whoever You mean to move.
And when the answer comes, do not let me call it luck.
In Jesus' name, amen.

headline: ONE PINT OF CORNMEAL|LEFT. HER LITTLE GIRL|*HOPED FOR POTATOES.*|THEN MORNING CAME.
caption:
A widow on the western prairie, four children, almost no work. One night there was a pint of cornmeal in the house and nothing else.

"Well, children," she said, "maybe the Lord will provide something."

"I do hope it will be a good mess of potatoes," said little Nell. "Seems to me I never was so hungry for taters before."

The mother lay awake, turning it over. Then, she said, the sweetest peace came over her and she slept.

In the morning she opened the door to go down to the brook. On the bench beside it stood pails of potatoes and a sack filled with flour.

She clapped her hands and shouted for the children, who came tumbling out half dressed, "like a flock of quails."

She washed the pails and set them back on the bench that night. By morning they were gone. She never learned who left them.

"The Lord never seemed so far off after that time," she said.

Nell asked for potatoes. Nell got potatoes.

caption:
Charles Spurgeon prayed this out loud, in front of thousands, in Victorian London. Read it slowly.

"We can truly say that we delight in God. There was a time when we feared Thee, O God, with the fear of bondage. Now we reverence, but we love as much as we reverence. The thought of Thine omnipresence was once horrible to us. We said, “Whither shall we flee from His presence?” and it seemed to make hell itself more dreadful, because we heard a voice, “If I make my bed in hell, behold, Thou art there.” But now, O Lord, we desire to find Thee. Our longing is to feel Thy presence and it is the heaven of heavens that Thou art there. The sick bed is soft when Thou art there. The furnace of affliction grows cool when Thou art there and the house of prayer, when Thou art present, is none other than the house of God and it is the very gate of heaven."

Which line is yours today?

headline: THREE MONTHS, NO RAIN.|A SCOFFER MOCKED THE|PREACHER. *HE RAN HOME*|*AND FELL ON HIS KNEES.*
caption:
The fields around Oberlin were dying. For nearly three months every cloud that promised rain drifted out over Lake Erie and emptied itself there.

Charles Finney was out walking, watching another dark bank sit uselessly over the water, when a man named Ralph stopped him. How could Finney preach that God was always wise and always good, he demanded, while He poured rain on a lake and let them suffer for want of it?

Finney said the words cut him to the heart. He did not argue. He turned and ran home, shut himself in, and pleaded with God to answer for the honor of His own name.

"Before I rose from my knees," he said, "there was a sound of a rushing, mighty wind."

He looked out. The sky was black. The cloud was rolling in off the lake.

It rained in torrents for two full hours.

A professor who was there that day confirmed it years later. He remembered the cloud. He had been driven to his knees too.

headline: HE RENTED A ROOM TO|PRAY AT LUNCH HOUR.|FOR THIRTY MINUTES|*NOBODY CAME.*
caption:
September 23, 1857. Jeremiah Lanphier, a businessman turned city missionary, had handed out flyers all over lower Manhattan inviting merchants and clerks to a noon prayer meeting in an upper room on Fulton Street.

At twelve o'clock he was the only one there.

Twelve-ten. Twelve-twenty. He prayed by himself.

At half past, he heard a step on the stairs. Then another. By one o'clock there were six men in the room.

The next week there were twenty. The week after, forty. They decided to meet every day.

That same autumn a financial panic closed banks and threw thousands out of work. The room filled. Then the building. Then other churches and theaters across the city. Within months, by the usual count, some ten thousand people were stopping to pray in New York every day at noon, and the movement was spreading city to city.

It began with one man who kept praying for thirty minutes in an empty room.

If you are in the empty-room part of your story, stay.

headline: When did God answer *at the last minute?*
caption:
The old books are full of it: the flour that came the day the barrel was empty, the letter already on the desk.

When did it happen to you?

headline: Someone *Who Is Sick*
attribution: Come, divine Physician. The sick bed is soft when You are there.
caption:
A prayer for someone who is sick.

Lord Jesus, You know the name on my heart.
Come, divine Physician.
Give wisdom to every doctor and nurse who touches them. Guide the hands, the tests, the decisions.
Heal, Lord. We ask it plainly, because You told us to ask.
And while we wait, be in that room. The sick bed is soft when You are there.
Hold the one who is suffering. Hold the ones who are watching.
In Jesus' name, amen.

headline: THROWN OUT OF THE CITY|AT NIGHT, HE SAW ONE|LIGHT. INSIDE, A MAN|*WAS PRAYING FOR HIM.*
caption:
A Dutch preacher was holding a meeting in a city where he knew no one. Mid-sermon, a police officer walked in, shut it down, and ordered him out of town.

It was dark. He had nowhere to go. He wandered near the city gates, steadying himself with the words, "Lo, I am with you always."

Then he noticed a light in the distance and walked toward it. Perhaps, he thought, the Lord has a shelter for me there.

As he reached the house he heard a voice. A man was praying aloud. The preacher stopped at the door and listened.

"Lord Jesus, one of Thy persecuted servants may be wandering at this moment in a strange place of which he knows nothing. May he find my home, that he may receive here food and lodging."

He waited for the "Amen." Then he stepped inside.

The two men dropped to their knees together.

Someone may be praying for you tonight who does not even know your name.

headline: HER TRUNKS WERE|ALREADY ON THE SHIP.|MID-PRAYER HE STOPPED:|*"YOU MUST NOT GO."*
caption:
A young woman in Liverpool had booked passage to join her family in Jamaica. Her luggage was aboard. The ship sailed in the morning.

Before leaving she called on her minister, William Bramwell, to say goodbye and ask for his prayers. They knelt, and he began commending her to God's care for the voyage.

Then he went quiet.

"My dear sister, you must not go tomorrow. God has just told me you must not go."

She was stunned. Everything was arranged. But he would not be moved, and at last she gave in. He went down to the docks himself and helped carry her trunks back off the vessel.

The ship sailed without her.

About six weeks later the news reached Liverpool. It had gone down. Everyone on board was lost.

Not every closed door is a punishment. Some of them are a rescue.

Which closed door are you thankful for now?

headline: SPURGEON'S COLLEGE|WAS OUT OF MONEY.|A FRIEND SAID,|*"OPEN YOUR LETTERS."*
caption:
Charles Spurgeon told this one himself, from his own pulpit.

His college for training young ministers had been running about a year when the money ran out. One Sunday evening he paid away the last he had.

"There is nothing left, whatever," he told a friend.

"You have a good banker, sir."

"Yes, and I should like to draw upon Him now, for I have nothing."

"Have you prayed about it?" He had. "Then leave it with Him. Have you opened your letters?"

Spurgeon did not open mail on Sundays. "Open them for once," said his friend.

The first envelope was from a bank. A lady, completely unknown to them, had left two hundred pounds for him to use in educating young men.

"Such a sum has never come since, and it never came before," Spurgeon said. He never found out who she was. "To me it seemed that it came directly from God."

The answer was already on his desk.

headline: HE GAVE A BEGGAR HIS|LAST THREE COINS. THEN|HE PRAYED, *"LORD, I LENT*|*THEM TO YOU."*
caption:
Michael Feneberg was the pastor of Seeg, in Bavaria. One day a traveler with an empty purse begged him for three crowns to finish his journey.

It was all the money Feneberg had. But the man asked in the name of Jesus, so in the name of Jesus he gave it.

Almost at once he found himself in real need, with no way out. So he prayed the way a child talks to a father:

"Lord, I lent Thee three crowns. Thou hast not yet returned them, and Thou knowest how I need them. Lord, I pray Thee, give them back."

That same day a letter arrived with money in it. The traveler had told his story to a rich man, who sent a gift for the generous vicar.

Two hundred thalers. For three crowns.

The old pastor laughed out loud in amazement. "Ah, dear Lord, one dare ask nothing of Thee, for straightway Thou makest one feel so much ashamed!"

You cannot out-give God. People keep trying.

headline: A THIEF DROVE OFF|WITH HIS SLEIGH.|HE PRAYED *FOR THE*|*THIEF'S CONSCIENCE.*
caption:
Marshfield, Vermont, about 1829. A man calling himself John Cotton had been in town six weeks, selling wooden clocks. He borrowed a neighbor's sleigh and harness for a three-day trip.

He did not come back. It turned out he had bought the clocks on credit, sold them all, and owed for his horse besides.

The owner felt it badly. They had little, and what they had came from hard labor. Chasing him was pointless.

About three weeks later he came in one evening, perfectly calm. "I shall not worry any more about my sleigh and harness. I think I shall get them again."

His wife asked why.

"I have been praying to God to arrest Cotton's conscience, so that he will be obliged to leave them where I can get them."

Six days later a letter came from an innkeeper forty miles off, in Littleton, New Hampshire. A man had ridden in at midnight, refused a bed, and insisted on leaving a sleigh and harness for a Mr. P. of Marshfield. He rode away at two in the morning on one of the coldest nights of the year.

He paid nobody else he owed. Only that.

headline: A HUNGRY LITTLE GIRL|WALKED INTO A BAKERY|AND SAID,|*"I'VE COME FOR IT."*
caption:
Nettie lived in an attic with a mother too sick to work. There was no bread. So she knelt by the bed and said, slowly, "Give us this day our daily bread."

Then she went out to find where God kept it.

Around the corner was a baker's shop with full shelves. This must be the place, she thought. She walked in.

"I've come for it."

"Come for what?"

"My daily bread. I'll take two, if you please. One for mother and one for me."

He bagged them. She turned to go. "Stop, you little rogue! Where is your money?"

She had none. He called her a thief. She burst into tears and told him everything: her mother, the prayer, how she thought God meant her to come and fetch it.

The baker was a rough man. He was not a hard one.

"You poor, dear girl. Here, take this to your mother." He filled a large basket and put it in her arms.

She asked for two loaves. She went home with a basketful.

headline: A FARMER STOPPED|HALFWAY TO HIS FIELD.|*"I HAVE TO GO BACK,"*|HE TOLD HIS MEN.
caption:
A young minister and his wife were sent to their first charge in Vermont around 1846. Few members, most of them poor. Within months the couple had cooked the last food in the house.

They ate that final breakfast and prayed together. Then he went out to an old barn to lay it before God, and she did the same in her room.

That same morning, a mile or two off, a young farmer was heading to his mowing field with his hired hands. He stopped in the road. He told the men to go on without him. He had to go back, he said. He had to carry provisions to the minister's house.

He told his wife how he felt and asked her to help him pack. Potatoes, meat, flour, sugar, butter. A full wagon.

He was not even a church member.

He drove up to the parsonage with no idea that two people inside were on their knees.

The minister told this story himself until he died in 1875. Then his wife kept telling it.

headline: "THERE'S NO WIND,"|THE MILLER SAID.|*"SPREAD THE SAILS,"*|SAID SAMMY. *"I'LL PRAY."*
caption:
Samuel Hick, a Yorkshire blacksmith, had promised two loads of corn for a church gathering at Micklefield. The day was close, there was no flour in the house, and the country had been becalmed so long that every windmill stood with its arms out, catching nothing.

Sammy carried his corn to the nearest mill anyway and asked the miller to unfurl his sails.

"There's no wind."

"I will go and pray while you spread the cloth."

The miller did it mostly to humor him. The canvas was barely stretched when a fine breeze came up. The sails spun. The corn became meal. Sammy shouldered it and went home rejoicing.

A neighbor had seen the mill turning and hurried over with corn of his own. Too late. The air was dead again.

The miller shrugged. "You must send for Sammy Hick to pray for the wind to blow again."

God is not short of wind. He may be waiting for someone to spread the sails.

headline: THE LEAK STOPPED AND|NO ONE KNEW WHY. THEN|THEY *TURNED THE SHIP*|*UPSIDE DOWN.*
caption:
The crossing from Liverpool to Bermuda should have taken weeks. It took six months.

Fog swallowed the ship. Winds threw her every direction. Captain and mate lost their reckoning. Then she sprang a leak, and they gave up.

Crew and passengers were down to a few drops of water and one potato a day. They sat waiting to starve or drown.

All but one. A minister on board kept insisting they would be saved, his confidence burning brighter as everyone else's went out.

A few days before they sighted land, the leak suddenly stopped. No one could explain it.

A week after they limped into harbor, the ship was condemned as unseaworthy. Before she was broken up, someone proposed turning her over to see what had plugged the hole.

That end of the hull was covered, completely, with barnacles.

Nobody on board had lifted a finger. The repair crew had been sent from underneath.

headline: SEVEN LETTERS LAY ON|HIS DESK. AFTER FIVE,|HE TOLD HIS WIFE:|*"PUT THEM INTO THE FIRE."* || He ran a home for three hundred epileptic patients, entirely on faith. He was five hundred pounds in debt and had not slept. || The first five letters were all pleas to take in more patients. He could not bear another one. He headed for the door. || "John," said his wife, *"this won't do. Come back."* || Letter six: a check from a stranger for three hundred pounds. Letter seven: *exactly the rest.* Just that and no more. || The answer was in the two envelopes he almost burned. *What have you stopped opening?*
caption:
This was told at a gathering in Paris by the man it happened to, a pastor who had founded a home for epileptic patients at La Force and ran it the way George Muller ran his orphanages: no appeals, only prayer.

He was honest about that morning. He did not meet it with heroic faith. He quit.

His wife called him back to the desk.

Sometimes the person God uses to answer your prayer is the one who will not let you walk away from it.

headline: HE STEERED FOR AN|EMPTY ISLAND AGAINST|ALL REASON. *SIXTEEN*|*MEN WERE WAITING.*
caption:
Admiral Sir Thomas Williams was crossing the Atlantic when Ascension Island showed as a smudge on the horizon. It was uninhabited then. Ships went there for turtles and nothing else.

As he looked at it, he was seized by a desire he could not account for: steer toward it.

He knew how that would sound to his crew, so he tried to ignore it. It only grew stronger. Finally he told his lieutenant to put the ship about.

The officer objected, respectfully. It would cost them time. The men were just sitting down to dinner. Could it not wait?

The arguments only made the captain more anxious. The ship turned.

Every spyglass on deck was soon trained on the shore. "It is white. It is a flag. It must be a signal!"

Sixteen men had been wrecked there many days before. They were starving. They had put up the flag almost without hope that anyone would ever see it.

Someone did. He just did not know why he was looking.

alt_text: Illustrated scene with the headline: HE STEERED FOR AN EMPTY ISLAND AGAINST ALL REASON. SIXTEEN MEN WERE WAITING.

caption:
For everyone who is tired of being strong. This is Charles Spurgeon, praying for his congregation:

"Our Father, come and rest Thy children now. Take the helmet from our brow, remove from us the weight of our heavy armour for awhile, and may we just have peace, perfect peace, and be at rest. Oh! help us, we pray Thee, now. As Thou hast already washed Thy people in the fountain filled with blood and they are clean, now this morning wash us from defilement in the water. With the basin and with the ewer, O Master, wash our feet again. It will greatly refresh. It will prepare us for innermost fellowship with Thyself. So did the priests wash ere they went into the holy place."

Read it once more as your own prayer.
first_comment: Source: the recorded pulpit prayers of Charles Haddon Spurgeon (1834-1892). Public domain. Quoted word for word.

headline: Prayer is to move and oblige ourselves, *not to move or oblige God.*
caption:
We do not pray to talk God into being good. He already is.

We pray, Henry says, to move ourselves: toward trust, toward surrender, toward Him.
first_comment: Source: Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), "To the Reader." Public domain. Quoted word for word.
alt_text: Quote card reading: Prayer is to move and oblige ourselves, not to move or oblige God. - Matthew Henry

headline: In mental prayer *thoughts are words,* and they are the first-born of the soul.
caption: For the days you have no words. The thought you turned toward God in the hospital hallway counted. He heard it as clearly as a sermon.
first_comment: Source: Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), "To the Reader." Public domain. Quoted word for word.
alt_text: Quote card reading: In mental prayer thoughts are words, and they are the first-born of the soul. - Matthew Henry

headline: HE STEPPED ONTO SNOW|WITH NOTHING UNDER IT.|FAR AWAY, A SICK WOMAN|*WAS PRAYING THAT HOUR.*
caption:
Two brothers were climbing in the Monte Rosa range. Near the top they walked into dense fog.

The guides suddenly turned and planted their axes. One brother, seeing what looked like more slope ahead, pushed on past them. He did not know he was walking onto a cornice, a lip of snow hanging over a drop of several thousand feet.

The guides screamed.

He stood for a moment on the very edge. Then the snow gave way and he began to go through.

One guide lunged after him, at the risk of his own life, caught him by the coat, and dragged him back.

The man was a minister. When he got home, an invalid in his congregation told him she had been praying for his safety, and that at one particular hour she had felt driven to plead for him as if he were in terrible danger.

They compared the times.

They matched.

You may never know, this side of heaven, what your prayers held back.
first_comment: Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("Rescued in Peril"). Retold here in modern English.
alt_text: Illustrated scene with the headline: HE STEPPED ONTO SNOW WITH NOTHING UNDER IT. FAR AWAY, A SICK WOMAN WAS PRAYING THAT HOUR.

headline: THE TORNADO FLATTENED|EVERY TREE AROUND HER.|*EXCEPT THE ONE*|*SHE PRAYED FOR.*
caption:
The storm cut a path through the country that the old account puts at a mile wide. Trees were torn up by the roots. Barns and fences went flat.

Right in the middle of that path stood a small cabin. An elderly widow lived there with her only son.

In front of the cabin was one large tree. The wind caught it and began twisting and thrashing it. If it came down, it would come down on the house.

Everywhere around her, great trees were falling.

She could not hold up a tree. She could not move her house. So she did the one thing left. She knelt and asked the God who "gathereth the wind in his fists" to spare that tree.

When it was over, it was still standing.

It was the only tree left standing for a considerable distance around her cabin.

She did not ask Him to stop the storm. She asked Him for one tree.

Sometimes the prayer is not "take this away." It is "keep this one thing standing."
first_comment: Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts. Retold here in modern English. Image: Martin Johnson Heade, Approaching Thunder Storm, 1859. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Open Access (public domain).
alt_text: Illustrated scene with the headline: THE TORNADO FLATTENED EVERY TREE AROUND HER. EXCEPT THE ONE SHE PRAYED FOR.

headline: Who taught you *how to pray?*
caption:
Matthew Henry learned at his father's table. Spurgeon never forgot hearing his mother pray for him by name.

Who was it for you?
alt_text: Question card reading: Who taught you how to pray?

headline: The One Who Feels *Forgotten*
attribution: Mamma, are you there? Yes, darling.
caption:
A prayer for when God feels far away.

Lord, I am calling up the stairs like a child:
Are You there?
I cannot hear You the way I used to. The heavens feel shut.
But You said, "I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee," and You do not lie.
So I will take Your word over my feelings tonight.
I am not asking for a sign. I am asking for the grace to keep on with what You have given me to do, knowing You are in the house.
Answer me from Your Word. That is enough.
In Jesus' name, amen.

There is an old story of a small child playing downstairs who kept stopping to call, "Mamma, are you there?" "Yes, darling." "All right." And went back to playing.

alt_text: Prayer card titled: The One Who Feels Forgotten

headline: SHE HAD NO SHOES FOR|CHURCH, SO SHE PRAYED.|*A YOUNG TEACHER RODE*|*TWO MILES THAT DAY.*
caption:
She was a widow with an invalid son, and she had stopped going to church and to the neighborhood prayer meeting. Not for lack of wanting to. For lack of shoes.

So she asked the Lord for a pair.

That very day the village schoolmaster stopped in to see her boy. He noticed her shoes. He said nothing. But he could not shake it.

He hired a horse, rode two miles to a shoe store, bought a pair, and asked that they be sent to her cottage without delay.

They fit perfectly.

That night she hurried to the prayer meeting to tell everyone that the Lord had sent her shoes.

The young schoolmaster was sitting in the room. He heard every word. He went home, the account says, and wet his pillow with tears of gratitude that God had used him to answer a widow's prayer.

He was an old, white-haired man when he finally told the story.

You might be the answer to a prayer you will hear about tonight.

headline: ...that not the least fragment of praying time may be lost. || Thirty seconds at a red light counts. *Use the scraps.*
caption:
Henry is talking about the small gaps: the pause while someone else is praying, the minute before the meal.

He treated them like a tailor treats cloth. Nothing wasted.
first_comment: Source: Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), "To the Reader." Public domain. Quoted word for word.
alt_text: Image reading: ...that not the least fragment of praying time may be lost. / Thirty seconds at a red light counts. Use the scraps. - Matthew Henry

headline: We are not straitened in Him, why then should we be *stinted and straitened* in our own bosoms?
caption:
"Straitened" is an old word for squeezed tight.

Henry's point: God is not stingy. The smallness is all on our end. We ask for crumbs from a Father who set the table.
first_comment: Source: Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), "To the Reader." Public domain. Quoted word for word.
alt_text: Quote card reading: We are not straitened in Him, why then should we be stinted and straitened in our own bosoms? - Matthew Henry

headline: A man may write straight *without having his paper ruled.*
caption:
Henry wrote a whole book of prayer outlines, and then said this about it.

Use the lines if they help. But you do not need a formula to talk to your Father.
first_comment: Source: Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), "To the Reader." Public domain. Quoted word for word.
alt_text: Quote card reading: A man may write straight without having his paper ruled. - Matthew Henry

headline: THE LANDLORD SAID,|"GET OUT." HER LITTLE|GIRL WENT TO ASK GOD|*FOR A HOME.*
tag: As told by D. L. Moody
caption:
D. L. Moody used to tell about a family at the start of the Civil War. The father had joined the army. A few days later the landlord came for the rent, and the mother did not have it.

He stormed. They would have to leave. He was not going to keep people who could not pay.

When he was gone she dropped into a chair and wept.

Her little girl came over. "What makes you cry, mamma? I will pray to God to give us a little home, and won't He?"

What could her mother say? The child went into the next room. The door was open.

"O God, you have come and taken away father, and mamma has got no money, and the landlord will turn us out, and we will have to sit on the doorstep, and mamma will catch cold. Give us a little home."

A pause. Then: "Won't you, please, God?"

She came out perfectly happy.

The landlord's heart changed. Moody said that mother never paid rent again.

headline: He maketh the storm a calm, so that *the waves thereof are still.* || Thunder broke over an Indiana camp meeting. The cloud split in two and passed on either side. Not one drop fell on the camp.
caption:
The preacher that day was an old man they called Father Haven. He stopped, prayed, and told the crowd to keep their seats.

More on him soon.

headline: What would you say to someone who has *stopped praying?*
caption:
Not a lecture. What would you actually say to them across a kitchen table?

They may be reading this.
alt_text: Question card reading: What would you say to someone who has stopped praying?

headline: Courage *To Wait*
attribution: Lord, keep me from sailing out of the place where You are holding me.
caption:
A prayer for the waiting room.

Father, I have asked, and the answer has not come, and I am tired of this place.
If You are holding me here, as You once held a ship in still water while a hurricane passed, then hold me.
Keep me from forcing a door You have closed.
Keep me from calling Your delay a denial.
Give me something useful to do while I wait.
And when the mist lifts, let me be found standing on deck with the instrument in my hand, expecting You.
In Jesus' name, amen.
first_comment: An original prayer. Draws on accounts in The Wonders of Prayer (1885).

headline: HE WROTE A TELEGRAM|BEGGING FOR PRAYER.|*IT WAS NEVER SENT.*|IT DIDN'T NEED TO BE.
caption:
A minister was traveling in Switzerland when his daughter fell so ill that the doctor gave up hope.

Far from home, he wanted his people praying. He decided to wire the New York prayer meeting where he had so often prayed for others. He wrote out the telegram and got ready to send it.

Then something happened he had never felt in his life. A flood of joyful confidence in God poured over him, so strong that he dropped to his knees and began to give thanks, certain his prayers for her life had been heard.

The telegram lay on the table.

In less than half an hour his wife came into the room. "There is a change for the better in our daughter."

He never sent it.

"I believe the writing of it was the prayer that God answered," he told that same meeting later.

Before they call, I will answer.
first_comment: Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("A Telegram of Prayer"). Retold here in modern English.
alt_text: Illustrated scene with the headline: HE WROTE A TELEGRAM BEGGING FOR PRAYER. IT WAS NEVER SENT. IT DIDN'T NEED TO BE.

headline: A STRANGER RODE UP|AT DAWN, HANDED HER|AN ENVELOPE AND|*LEFT WITHOUT A WORD.* || Her husband, a minister, lay sick in bed. A houseful of small children. That evening she told him she had broken their last dollar. || He lay awake most of the night, praying. || That same night, miles away, a man dreamed that a preacher who had once visited his church was *sick and in want.* He did not even know the man's name. || At first light he got the name and address from his own pastor, saddled his horse, and knocked *just as she raised the window shades.* || Ten dollars. While one man prayed in the dark, *God was waking another.*
caption:
Their child wrote this down years later.

Nobody in that house had told anyone about the last dollar. The rider did not stay to explain himself. The family only learned the rest of it afterward, from his pastor.

If someone keeps coming to your mind and you cannot say why, it may be worth getting on the horse.

headline: Our burdens, cares, and wants are many, *so are our sins and mercies.*
caption:
One sentence, four lists. Most of us only ever bring Him the first three words.

Try the last one today. Count the mercies.
first_comment: Source: Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), "To the Reader." Public domain. Quoted word for word.
alt_text: Quote card reading: Our burdens, cares, and wants are many, so are our sins and mercies. - Matthew Henry

headline: Our God gives liberally, and hath bid us *open our mouths wide,* and He will fill them.
caption:
Henry is leaning on Psalm 81:10.

What would you ask for if you actually believed this?
first_comment: Source: Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), "To the Reader." Public domain. Quoted word for word.
alt_text: Quote card reading: Our God gives liberally, and hath bid us open our mouths wide, and He will fill them. - Matthew Henry

headline: A WIDOW WEPT BESIDE|HER HUSBAND'S BODY.|HER SMALL SON ASKED,|*"IS GOD DEAD, MOTHER?"*
caption:
She was sitting in the room where her husband's body lay, crying.

Their only child came in. "Why do you weep so, mother?"

She told him. His father was gone. And then, because she could not help it, she told him the rest: they were poor now. She did not know how they would live.

The little boy looked up into her face.

"Is God dead, mother?"

That is the whole story as the old book tells it. No ending. No miracle. Just a question from a child that has been stopping grown believers in their tracks for a hundred and fifty years.

He was not minimizing her grief. He was reminding her who was still alive.

If you are afraid tonight about what comes next, ask yourself his question.

headline: NOT EVERY CLOSED DOOR IS A PUNISHMENT. *SOME ARE A RESCUE.*
caption:
A young woman in Liverpool was talked out of a voyage the night before she sailed. Six weeks later word came that the ship had gone down with everyone aboard.

Which closed door are you grateful for now?
first_comment: From "You Must Not Go" in The Wonders of Prayer (1885).
alt_text: Image reading: NOT EVERY CLOSED DOOR IS A PUNISHMENT. SOME ARE A RESCUE.
source: OR | From "You Must Not Go" in The Wonders of Prayer (1885)

headline: Morning or night: *when do you pray best?*
caption:
"The first hour of the morning is the rudder of the day," said Beecher. Some of us do better at midnight.

Which are you?
alt_text: Question card reading: Morning or night: when do you pray best?

headline: The *Grieving*
attribution: Lord, the chair is empty and You are not.
caption:
A prayer for those who are grieving.

Lord, the chair is empty.
I keep reaching for the phone to tell them something.
You wept at a grave, so I am not ashamed to weep in front of You.
I do not ask You to hurry me through this.
I ask You to walk it with me, at my pace.
Is God dead? No. Then I am not without hope, even here.
Hold the one I miss until I see them again.
In Jesus' name, amen.

If you are missing someone today, you can say their name here. It is good to say their name.

alt_text: Prayer card titled: The Grieving
source: OR | Draws on an account in the New Cyclopaedia of Prose Illustrations (1875)

headline: THE CAPTAIN SAID ALL|WERE LOST. A CABIN BOY|ANSWERED, *"GOD WILL*|*SAVE US YET."*
caption:
The storm had the ship on her beam ends, lying over on her side with the sea pouring across her. The captain looked at it and told everyone aboard the truth as he saw it: death was certain.

One voice disagreed. It belonged to a sailor boy who prayed.

"God will save us yet."

Nobody on that deck had reason to believe him. She seemed ready to go down at any second.

Then a great wave struck her. And instead of finishing her, it knocked her upright.

A few days later she rode safely into New York Harbor.

The same sea that was drowning them was the thing God used to set them on their feet.

The captain had the experience. The boy had the faith. Guess which one read the situation correctly.
first_comment: Source: New Cyclopaedia of Prose Illustrations (1875), public domain ("Faith, Safety of").
alt_text: Illustrated scene with the headline: THE CAPTAIN SAID ALL WERE LOST. A CABIN BOY ANSWERED, "GOD WILL SAVE US YET."

headline: THUNDER CRACKED AS HE|STOOD TO PREACH. HE SAID,|*"NOT ONE DROP WILL*|*FALL HERE TODAY."*
caption:
It was a camp meeting in southern Indiana, and it had rained nearly the whole week.

An old preacher they called Father Haven stood up and announced his text. Thunder answered him. The crowd shifted on the benches and looked at the sky.

"Let us engage a moment in prayer," he said.

He asked God to let the storm pass by and not disturb them. Then he looked up.

"Friends, keep your seats. It will not rain one drop here today."

He began to preach. It thundered again. He repeated what he had said. The cloud kept coming until it was nearly on top of them.

Then, the account says, it divided. Half went north and half went south, about a quarter of a mile off on either side. The two halves joined again beyond the camp and moved on.

"Not one solitary drop of rain fell on that encampment."

You can call it weather. The people sitting dry on those benches called it something else.
first_comment: Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("No Fear of Thunder"). Retold here in modern English. Image: William Keith, Approaching Storm, 1880. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Open Access (public domain).
alt_text: Illustrated scene with the headline: THUNDER CRACKED AS HE STOOD TO PREACH. HE SAID, "NOT ONE DROP WILL FALL HERE TODAY."

headline: Let Philip cease to *rule the world.*
caption:
Melanchthon, Luther's closest friend, was a worrier. When his fears ran away with him, the old books say, he would scold himself with this sentence.

Put your own name in it.
first_comment: Source: New Cyclopaedia of Prose Illustrations (1875), public domain ("Providence, Trusting").
alt_text: Quote card reading: Let Philip cease to rule the world. - Philip Melanchthon

headline: It lightens the stroke to *draw near to Him* who handles the rod.
tag: A sufferer, asked how he bore it so well
caption:
Our instinct in pain is to back away from God. This man, whose name nobody recorded, had learned the opposite.

The closer you stand, the lighter it falls.
first_comment: Source: New Cyclopaedia of Prose Illustrations (1875), public domain ("Affliction, Bearing").
alt_text: Quote card reading: It lightens the stroke to draw near to Him who handles the rod. - An afflicted believer

headline: HE OFFERED HER GOLD|*NOT TO PRAY*|FOR ONE DAY.|SHE DIDN'T HESITATE.
caption:
She was poor. Half a sovereign was real money to her, more than she might see in a long while.

A man offered it to her on one condition: go a whole day without praying.

Maybe he was testing her. Maybe he thought prayer was a habit like any other, and every habit has a price.

"No, sir! Not for all the worlds this side heaven."

And then, before he could say anything:

"But I'll just go ask the Lord to help you to believe on Him. And then you'll love prayer as much as I do."

He tried to buy one day of her silence. She answered by spending her prayer on him.

What would it take to get you to skip it? For a lot of us the honest answer is: a busy morning.
first_comment: Source: New Cyclopaedia of Prose Illustrations (1875), public domain ("Prayer, Love of").
alt_text: Illustrated scene with the headline: HE OFFERED HER GOLD NOT TO PRAY FOR ONE DAY. SHE DIDN'T HESITATE.

Four miles away a man *put two bushels of flour in a bag.* || A father wrote a telegram begging for prayer. His daughter turned the corner *before he could send it.* || >> "Before they call, *I will answer.*" Isaiah 65:24
caption:
Four accounts from one old book, all with the same shape: the answer left the station before the prayer was finished.

Has that ever happened to you?

headline: What did your *grandmother* pray that you still remember?
caption:
Some of us are still living on prayers that were prayed over us sixty years ago.

What do you remember?
alt_text: Question card reading: What did your grandmother pray that you still remember?

headline: A *Cold* Heart
attribution: We wish we loved You more. But You are very dear to us.
caption:
A prayer for when you do not feel like praying.

Lord, I will be honest. I do not feel much tonight.
The words are dry. My mind is everywhere else.
I am like a half-hatched bird, alive but stuck in the shell.
I wish I loved You more. But You are very dear to me, and I am here.
I am not going to wait until I feel something to come.
Take this small, cold offering and breathe on it.
If I think I love You more than I do, then let me yet love You more than I think.
In Jesus' name, amen.

headline: "I CAN'T STOP TO PRAY,"|SAID THE DEACON.|WHAT HE DID INSTEAD|*WAS THE PRAYER.*
caption:
A deacon in the Berkshire hills was out picking and barreling his early apples for the city market when someone came to ask for his prayers. A poor man with a large family had broken his leg.

"I can't stop now to pray," said the deacon.

Then he added:

"But you can go down into the cellar and get some corned beef, salt pork, potatoes, and butter. That's the best I can do."

The old editors printed that story without a word of comment. They did not need one.

There is a time to fold your hands. And there is a time when God has already put the answer in your cellar and is waiting for you to open the door.

Is there someone you have been praying for whom you could simply help?

caption:
The very first sentence of Henry's book on prayer.

He meant "business" the old way: the main thing you are here to do.

headline: We lie to God in prayer if we do not *rely upon Him after prayer.*
caption:
Praying about it and then carrying it right back out of the room with you.

Most of us know exactly what Swinnock means.
first_comment: Source: New Cyclopaedia of Prose Illustrations (1875), public domain ("Trust in God").
alt_text: Quote card reading: We lie to God in prayer if we do not rely upon Him after prayer. - George Swinnock

headline: I lay my head to rest on *the bosom of Omnipotence.*
caption:
Richard Cecil said he woke one morning with this line of Rutherford's running through his mind, and decided that while he could hold onto it, "it shall be a fine day, whether it rains, hails, or shines."

A pillow for tonight.

headline: AN ORPHAN'S FIRST NIGHT|IN A STRANGE HOUSE.|SHE ENDED HER PRAYER,|*"OF COURSE HE WILL."*
tag: As told by D. L. Moody
caption:
Moody told of a little girl whose father and mother had both died. Another family took her in.

That first night, in a strange room, she asked if she could pray the way she used to. They said yes.

She knelt and said the prayer her mother had taught her. Then she added one of her own.

"O God, make these people as kind to me as father and mother were."

She stopped and looked up, as if she were waiting for a reply.

Then she finished: "Of course He will."

Moody loved that. She did not say "if it be possible." She did not hedge. She asked her Father for something good, and then she answered for Him, because she knew Him.

She got what she asked.

When did we learn to pray with our fingers crossed?
first_comment: Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("Of Course He Will"). Retold here in modern English.
alt_text: Illustrated scene with the headline: AN ORPHAN'S FIRST NIGHT IN A STRANGE HOUSE. SHE ENDED HER PRAYER, "OF COURSE HE WILL."

caption:
A prayer for before you pray. Spurgeon, to his congregation, asking God to clear the room:

"Lord Jesus, take from us now everything that would hinder the closest communion with God. Any wish or desire that might hamper us in prayer remove, we pray Thee. Any memory of either sorrow or care that might hinder the fixing of our affection wholly on our God, take it away now. What have we to do with idols anymore? Thou hast seen and observed us. Thou knowest where the difficulty lies. Help us against it and may we now come boldly, not into the Holy place alone, but into the Holiest of all, where we should not dare to come if our great Lord had not rent the veil, sprinkled the mercy seat with His own blood, and bidden us enter."

What do you need Him to take away before you can come close?
first_comment: Source: the recorded pulpit prayers of Charles Haddon Spurgeon (1834-1892). Public domain. Quoted word for word.

headline: Has a stranger ever been *God's answer* to your need?
caption:
A schoolmaster once bought a widow a pair of shoes without knowing she had prayed for them that morning.

Has someone ever shown up for you like that?
alt_text: Question card reading: Has a stranger ever been God's answer to your need?

headline: Our Children and *Grandchildren*
attribution: Lord, let them know You younger than I did.
caption:
A prayer for the next generation.

Father, I bring You the children. You know each name.
Let them know You younger than I did, and love You longer.
Guard their eyes and their friendships.
Give them the faith of the little girl who walked through wolves and was not afraid.
Where I have failed them, be merciful, and mend what I marred.
Let my prayers outlive me and still be working when I am gone.
And bring every one of them home.
In Jesus' name, amen.

headline: "MOTHER, I THINK GOD|ALWAYS HEARS WHEN WE|*SCRAPE THE BOTTOM*|*OF THE BARREL."*
caption:
A little boy said that to his mother one day.

They were poor. More than once they had burned the last stick of wood and eaten the last bit of bread without any idea where the next would come from.

And more than once, right then, help had arrived from somewhere they never expected.

It had happened often enough that the boy had worked out a theology of it. He figured God must be listening for a particular sound: the scrape of a scoop on the bottom of an empty barrel.

The writer who recorded it said the boy was only putting in his own words what Abraham meant when he named a mountain Jehovah-Jireh. The Lord will provide.

Maybe you are hearing that scraping sound in your own house right now.

He hears it too.

headline: ONE DAY OF FIREWOOD|LEFT. HER UNBELIEVING|HUSBAND ASKED,|*"WHAT CAN BE DONE?"* || He was disabled and could not work. It was the dead of a northern winter. Aunt Sally said what she always said: *"The Lord will provide."* || He admitted she always said so, "and so it has always proved." *But this time he could see no way.* || "Nor do I," said Aunt Sally. *"But help will come.* God will not desert us." || Before the morning was over, the door opened. It was their son, a soldier they had not heard from in so long *they feared he was dead.* || By sundown he had cut and hauled a full supply of wood. His father said *he would never be distrustful again.*
caption:
Notice what Aunt Sally did not say. She did not claim to see how it would work out.

"Nor do I."

Faith is not knowing the way. It is knowing the One who has always found one.

caption:
A rudder is small. It still decides where the whole ship goes.

headline: NOT ONE SOUND WOKE HER.|SHE CARRIED THE LAST|ARMFUL IN *AS THE SKY*|*BROKE OPEN.*
caption:
Jennie and her elderly father lived at the very top of a four-story factory building, and they lived, the old account says, "by faith in Christ, from day to day; one hour at a time."

A lady visiting one morning was full of sympathy. She had thought of Jennie's big wash hanging on the roof when that drenching rain came through in the night. All that hard work, ruined.

"Oh, no, ma'am," said Jennie.

"The Lord woke me up out of a sound sleep, just as the first few drops fell. I hastened up and brought them all down nice and dry, and had only got to the foot of the stairs with the last armful when it poured down."

Then she explained why she was so sure.

"That was the Lord, ma'am. For there was not a single noise of any kind to waken me, and I was sound asleep."

Does God care about laundry? Jennie thought so. He cares about the woman who has to wash it.

headline: This poor man cried, and the LORD heard him, and *saved him out of all his troubles.* || A Vermont farmer prayed for a thief's conscience. Days later the thief left the stolen sleigh at an inn and rode off into the night.
caption:
He did not pray for revenge. He prayed that the man's conscience would not let him rest.

It didn't.

headline: What do you have today that you once *begged God for?*
caption:
The house. The child. The sobriety. The job. The peace.

It is easy to forget we prayed for what we now take for granted.
alt_text: Question card reading: What do you have today that you once begged God for?

headline: The One Who *Hurt You*
attribution: Lord, I cannot do this on my own. Forgive through me.
caption:
A prayer for the hardest forgiveness.

Lord, You know what they did. I do not have to explain it to You.
You also know I have replayed it more times than I can count.
I cannot make myself feel forgiveness. But I can make a decision in front of You, and I make it now.
I release them to You. You are a better judge than I am.
I ask You to bless them, and I ask You to help me mean it.
Do not let bitterness take root in me.
I have been forgiven much. Help me forgive.
In Jesus' name, amen.

headline: IS ANYTHING TOO SMALL|TO PRAY ABOUT?|SHE ASKED GOD TO FIND|*A SILVER THIMBLE.*
caption:
It was a silver thimble her mother had given her when she was a girl. She had used it for years. One day it was gone.

She searched everywhere, "long and faithfully." She cried a little. Finally she decided someone had taken it, or a child had carried it off, and she gave up.

She sat down to console herself. And a thought came: pray about it.

So she knelt. And while she was kneeling, she said, something whispered so plainly that she got straight up: look on the bed.

She went into her sister's room and turned back the spread. There it was, tucked in a fold of the quilt. She had lain down there that morning with the baby and it had slipped from her pocket.

"Thank God!" she said out loud.

It was only a thimble. But the God who counts the hairs on your head is not too busy for small things. He may be waiting for you to stop deciding what is too small to bring Him.

headline: "THERE WERE *SNAILS* IN THE ARK."
caption:
Sammy Hick, the Yorkshire blacksmith, once met a man so worn down he could barely walk the street. Sammy asked how he was getting on in his way to heaven.

"But slowly, I fear."

"Why, bless you, bairn. There were snails in the ark."

It took the snail a long time to get there. He got in the same as the eagle.

If your progress feels slow, this one is for you.

headline: Faith is like the magnetic needle — *often trembling, yet ever true.*
caption:
A compass needle shakes. It quivers at every roll of the ship. And it keeps pointing north.

Your faith is allowed to tremble. Trembling is not the same as turning.
first_comment: Source: New Cyclopaedia of Prose Illustrations (1875), public domain ("Faith").

headline: The withdrawal of the sunshine *leads us to look for the sun.*
caption:
Unbroken ease, Spurgeon said, makes us forget the Giver. It is often the gray season that sends us looking for Him again.

What did a hard year teach you to look for?

headline: HIS MOTHER WAS CRYING|OVER AN EMPTY PANTRY.|GEORGE, AGE FIVE:|*"I'VE JUST ASKED HIM."*
caption:
The family lived five or six miles from the nearest neighbor, and there were times they had almost nothing.

One day little George, four or five years old, found his mother in tears over it.

"Why, mother, don't cry any. We shall not starve. God will send us something to eat, I know He will. I've just been praying, and asked Him to."

The minister who recorded this said the boy believed it exactly as he would have if a dependable neighbor had promised to bring supper.

A day or two later, friends who lived at a distance and knew the family was poor pulled up with a surprise: a wagon-load of food and other comforts.

George grew up to be a minister. When the writer last asked after him, he was head of a school in the Southwest.

He started with one sentence most of us never quite learn to say: I've asked Him, so don't cry.

headline: THE CORN WAS DYING.|THE PILGRIMS STOPPED|AND *PRAYED ALL DAY.*|BY NIGHT IT RAINED.
caption:
Spring, 1623. The Plymouth settlers planted more corn than they ever had. By the time the seed was in the ground, their food was gone.

They lived on what one boat and one net could catch. When the fish failed they dug shellfish out of the sand. Every day they prayed, "Give us this day our daily bread," and every day, somehow, there was something.

Then came drought. By June the corn was withering and the grass looked like hay. Without a harvest, they would starve.

So they set apart a day to humble themselves and pray. They kept at it for eight or nine hours.

The morning was clear and hot. So was the whole forenoon.

Before night it began to rain.

Not a cloudburst that would have beaten the stalks flat. Gentle showers, which kept falling for many days, until the ground was soaked and the drooping corn stood up again.

Afterward they set apart another day. That one was for giving thanks.
